title: IT Helpdesk and Technical Support
summary: Learn to run a service desk: incidents, requests and SLAs, a step-by-step troubleshooting method, hardware and operating-system fixes, network troubleshooting, secure account and remote support, and excellent customer communication.
audience: Aspiring IT support technicians, students and staff who look after computers in schools and businesses

lessons.title: The service desk and IT service management

body.p: The IT service desk is the single point of contact between users and IT. Support analysts log every request, solve what they can on first contact and pass harder issues to specialist teams. Good support keeps people productive and builds trust in IT.

body.h: Key terms from IT service management

list: Incident: an unplanned interruption, such as "I can't print" or "email is down".
Service request: a standard ask, such as a new account, software install or password reset.
Problem: the underlying cause of one or more incidents, investigated so it stops recurring.
Change: a planned modification to systems, approved and scheduled to limit risk.
Tiers: tier 1 handles common issues, tier 2 deeper technical work, tier 3 specialists or vendors.

body.p: Priority combines impact (how many people or how critical) and urgency (how soon it hurts). A finance system down at month-end is high impact and high urgency; one user's slow laptop is low and low. Service level agreements (SLAs) set response and resolution targets. If 47 of 50 high-priority tickets met their target, SLA compliance is 47 / 50 = 94%.

body.tip: Log every request in the ticketing system, even quick ones. Unlogged work is invisible, and patterns in tickets reveal problems worth fixing.

body.p: Good technicians follow a method instead of guessing. A widely taught sequence is:

steps: Identify the problem: ask questions, reproduce it, note error messages and what changed recently.
Establish a theory of probable cause, starting with the simple and obvious.
Test the theory; if it is wrong, form a new one or escalate.
Plan the fix and consider its effects, such as downtime or data loss.
Implement the fix or escalate, then verify the system fully works.
Document the findings, actions and outcome.

list: When did it start, and what changed just before?
Does it affect one user, one room or everyone?
Can you show me exactly what happens?
Has a restart been tried?

body.p: Change one thing at a time and test after each change; otherwise you will not know what fixed it, and you may create new faults.

body.tip: If one user reports a fault, think device or account; if many report it at once, think network, server or a recent change.

body.p: Support analysts need a working knowledge of PC components and operating systems such as Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS.

list: CPU: runs instructions; overheating from dust or failed fans causes slowdowns and shutdowns.
RAM: working memory; too little makes systems slow when many programs are open. 8 GB is 8 x 1024 = 8192 MB in the binary units used by operating systems.
Storage: SSDs are much faster and more robust than hard disk drives; a failing disk may click or show read errors, so back up first.
Power: check cables, adapters and batteries before deeper diagnosis.
Peripherals: printers, monitors and docks cause many tickets; check drivers, cables and the correct default printer.
Restart: clears temporary faults and applies pending updates.
Update or roll back drivers and applications.
Check free disk space; a full disk breaks many programs.
Use built-in tools: Task Manager or Activity Monitor for runaway processes, Event Viewer or system logs for errors.
Reinstall software, or reimage a device from a standard image when faults are widespread.

body.tip: Before any repair that might lose data, confirm the user's files are backed up.

body.p: "The internet is down" is one of the most common tickets. Work from the device outwards.

list: IP address: identifies a device on a network. A home or office network 192.168.1.0/24 has 254 usable addresses; a smaller /26 network has 62.
An address beginning 169.254 means the device failed to get an address from the DHCP server.
DNS turns names like example.com into IP addresses; if IP addresses work but names do not, suspect DNS.
ipconfig (Windows) or ip addr (Linux) shows the device's address; ping tests whether another device replies; tracert or traceroute shows the path; nslookup tests DNS.

steps: Check physical links: cable plugged in, Wi-Fi on, correct network selected.
Check the device has a valid IP address (not 169.254.x.x).
Ping a public IP address to test internet connectivity.
Ping a name to test DNS.
If others are affected too, check the router, switch or internet provider status.

body.tip: Ask whether other users or devices nearby have the same problem; it quickly tells you whether the fault is local or wider.

body.p: Password resets, locked accounts and access requests are daily tasks, and they are also targets for attackers who pretend to be users. Always verify identity using an approved method before resetting a password or granting access.

list: Follow the least-privilege principle: grant only the access approved by the right manager.
Disable accounts promptly when staff leave.
Never ask users for their passwords; administrators can reset them instead.
Recognise and report phishing and suspicious calls (social engineering).
Keep devices patched, encrypted and protected by anti-malware.

body.p: Remote-access tools let analysts see and control a user's screen. Use only approved tools, ask the user's permission, tell them what you are doing, and end the session when finished. Scammers often call people pretending to be "IT support" to install remote-access software, so teach users to check who is calling.

body.tip: Write down the identity-verification steps and follow them every time, even for the CEO; attackers rely on people making exceptions.

body.p: Technical skill is only half of support. Users are often stressed, so listen fully, show empathy, avoid jargon and explain what you will do and when. Set honest expectations and keep users updated until the ticket is closed.

list: Record symptoms, error messages, steps already tried, the fix and the result.
Turn repeated fixes into knowledge-base articles with clear steps and screenshots.
Self-service articles let users fix simple problems, such as connecting to Wi-Fi, without waiting.
First contact resolution: if 360 of 450 tickets were solved on first contact, that is 80%.
Average response and resolution times, compared with SLAs.
Customer satisfaction surveys after tickets close.
Ticket trends by category, which point to problems worth fixing permanently.

body.p: Service desk roles lead to careers in networking, systems administration, cloud and cybersecurity. Entry-level certifications in IT support and networking help, together with hands-on practice.

body.tip: Close each ticket by confirming with the user that the problem is solved, not just that you made a change.

quiz.q: "Please create an email account for a new employee" is:
What is a problem in IT service management?
options: The underlying cause of one or more incidents

quiz.q: 47 of 50 tickets met the SLA. What is SLA compliance?
What is the first step of the troubleshooting method?
Why change only one thing at a time?
options: So you know what fixed the issue

quiz.q: How many megabytes is 8 GB in binary units?
How many usable host addresses does 192.168.1.0/24 have?
A PC shows an IP address of 169.254.10.4. This usually means:
options: It failed to get an address from DHCP

quiz.q: Websites open by IP address but not by name. Suspect:
Before resetting a password over the phone you must:
options: Email it to anyone who asks

quiz.q: Why disable accounts promptly when staff leave?
360 of 450 tickets were resolved on first contact. The first contact resolution rate is:

options: Clear steps to solve a recurring issue
